texto: I ran out of gas on a state highway in Nevada a
little after ten at night, about forty miles
from the nearest town.
That part was my fault.
I was twenty-two, driving from Reno to see my sister in Arizona, and I'd skipped the
last station because the prices were ridiculous
and I was sure there'd be another one soon.
There wasn't.
The car started sputtering on a long straight stretch
with nothing on either side but sagebrush
and dark hills.
I coasted onto the shoulder and sat there with
my hazards on, listening to the engine
tick as it cooled.
I had one bar of signal.
I called roadside assistance, gave them the
mile marker from my map app, and the woman
on the phone told me a tow truck would be there in about ninety minutes.
She asked if I felt safe.
I said, yes, because what else are you supposed to say?
The first thing I noticed was how quiet it was.
When the engine stopped ticking, there was nothing.
No wind, no insects, no traffic.
I could hear my own breathing.
Every few minutes, I'd turn the key just far
enough to check the time on the dashboard,
then turned it off again to save the battery.
I had half a bottle of water and a bag of sunflower seeds, and I remember rationing
the water like I was in a survival movie, which is funny now.
Around eleven, I saw a light out in the desert.
It was far off to the right, maybe a mile or
two, low to the ground, like a flashlight
or a lantern.
It didn't move for a long time.
Then it went out, and a few seconds later it came back on, closer.
I told myself it was a ranch house, or a radio tower, something on a timer.
I stopped looking at it after that, because every
time I looked, it seemed a little nearer,
and I didn't like the way that made me feel.
About thirty minutes in, headlights came up behind me.
My stomach dropped, but then I saw the light bar on the roof.
It was a sheriff's deputy.
He pulled in behind me and walked up with a flashlight,
an older guy with a gray mustache
and a tired, friendly face.
I explained what happened.
He shook his head and laughed a little, not
in a mean way, and said I wasn't the first
and wouldn't be the last.
He went back to his car and came back with two bottles of water.
Then he leaned down to my window, and his voice changed a little.
He said, listen, keep your doors locked until the tow gets here.
If anybody walks up to the car, you don't roll
the window down, you call 911, and you
tell them Deputy Harlan is out here.
I asked him if something had happened out here.
He looked down the road for a second, then back at me.
He said, people walk this road at night sometimes.
I don't stop for them anymore.
Then he told me to have a good night, got back in his cruiser, and pulled away.
I watched his taillights for a long time, until
they turned into one red dot, and then
nothing.
I called my sister to tell her what was going on.
The call dropped twice before it connected, and
when it did, the line was full of static,
like she was standing in wind.
I told her I'd run out of gas and that a deputy had stopped.
She asked if I was okay, and I said yes.
Then she asked who was with me.
I said nobody.
She was quiet for a second, and then she said
she could have sworn she heard someone in
The call dropped again, and I couldn't get it back.
After that, the quiet felt different.
I locked the doors and checked them twice.
I sat with my phone in my lap and kept looking in the side mirrors.
The road behind me was a straight black line under the stars.
I could see maybe a quarter mile back, and then it disappeared into the dark.
I told myself the deputy was just being careful,
and he probably said that to everyone.
I tried playing a podcast, but I turned it off
after a minute because I didn't like not
being able to hear.
At some point, I heard gravel crunch somewhere
behind the car, just once, the way it sounds
when someone shifts their weight.
I turned on my headlights and stared into the mirrors until my eyes watered.
There was nothing back there.
I told myself it was an animal, a coyote or a jackrabbit,
but I noticed I'd stopped breathing
while I listened, and I had to remind myself to start again.
The tow truck showed up about an hour after the deputy left.
I almost cried when I saw the amber lights.
The driver backed up in front of my car, got out, and gave me a wave.
He was a big guy in a reflective vest, probably in his fifties.
His name was Manny.
He told me to stay in the car while he hooked it up.
It would only take a few minutes.
I nodded and stayed put.
I was watching him in my headlights, crouched
down at the front of my car, working with
the chains.
And then I looked in my rearview mirror.
There was a woman standing behind my car.
She wasn't on the road.
She was on the shoulder, maybe ten feet back, at
the edge of the red glow from my tail lights.
She was older, maybe sixties, thin, with long gray hair and a hiking backpack.
She wasn't wearing a coat, and it was cold enough
that I had the heat on until the battery
scared me.
I hadn't seen any headlights.
I hadn't heard footsteps on the gravel.
She was just there.
She didn't look lost or scared.
She didn't look like someone whose car had broken down.
Her clothes were clean.
Her hair wasn't moving in the wind.
She stood there with her hands at her sides,
completely still, the way people stand in
an elevator waiting for the doors to open.
I didn't move.
I watched her in the mirror.
She walked up along the passenger side of the
car, slowly, and stopped at the back door.
Then she reached out and pulled the handle.
It was locked.
She pulled it again, harder, and the whole car rocked a little.
Then she bent down and looked through the back window.
She wasn't looking at me.
She was looking at the back seat, like she expected someone to be sitting there.
That was the part that stuck with me later.
She wasn't checking whether anyone was in the front.
She didn't care that I was sitting right there.
She was looking at the empty back seat with this
patient, almost hopeful expression, like
she was waiting for someone she knew to sit up and unlock the door for her.
I hit the horn.
I don't know why.
It was the only thing I could think of.
Manny stood up in front of the car.
The woman straightened up and walked to my window,
the passenger side, and knocked on
the glass with one knuckle, very politely.
She leaned down and said,
My car's just up the road.
I've got a flat.
I just need a ride to it.
Her voice was normal.
That's what I keep coming back to.
It was a completely normal voice.
A little hoarse, like somebody's grandmother.
I shook my head.
She smiled at me and said,
It's right up there and pointed down the highway, in the direction I'd been driving.
Manny was walking around the front of my car now, saying,
Hey, hey, ma'am.
I looked at him for maybe a second.
When I looked back at the window, she wasn't there.
I turned all the way around in my seat.
The shoulder was empty.
The road was empty.
Manny walked all the way around my car with his flashlight.
He walked back along the shoulder, maybe 50 yards.
There was nothing out there.
No footprints that we could see.
No sound.
Nothing.
The desert was flat for miles.
There wasn't anywhere for a person to go.
When he came back, he was breathing hard.
And he kept his flashlight pointed at the ground near his boots,
like he didn't want to see anything else with it.
He asked me if she'd touched the car.
I told him she'd pulled on the back door.
He walked around to that side and looked at the handle for a long time,
without touching it.
He came back to my window and asked if I was okay.
I told him what she'd said,
that her car was just up the road with a flat.
He didn't say anything for a second.
Then he asked me to ride up in the truck with him.
And he didn't really make it sound like a question.
We drove for about 20 minutes before either of us talked.
We passed the place where she'd pointed.
We passed the next five miles after that.
There was no car on the side of that road.
There was nothing.
Finally, Manny said,
She tell you it was a flat?
I said yes.
He nodded and kept his eyes on the road.
He said,
You're the third one this year, she's told that too.
The other two opened the door.
I asked him what happened to them.
He didn't answer me.
He just turned the radio on.
